## Abstract

While deep learning has revolutionized protein structure prediction, almost all experimentally characterized de novo protein designs have been generated using physically based approaches such as Rosetta. Here we describe a deep learning based protein sequence design method, ProteinMPNN, with outstanding performance in both in silico and experimental tests. The amino acid sequence at different positions can be coupled between single or multiple chains, enabling application to a wide range of current protein design challenges. On native protein backbones, ProteinMPNN has a sequence recovery of 52.4%, compared to 32.9% for Rosetta. Incorporation of noise during training improves sequence recovery on protein structure models, and produces sequences which more robustly encode their structures as assessed using structure prediction algorithms. We demonstrate the broad utility and high accuracy of ProteinMPNN using X-ray crystallography, cryoEM and functional studies by rescuing previously failed designs, made using Rosetta or AlphaFold, of protein monomers, cyclic homo-oligomers, tetrahedral nanoparticles, and target binding proteins.

**One-sentence summary** A deep learning based protein sequence design method is described that is widely applicable to current design challenges and shows outstanding performance in both in silico and experimental tests.

## Abstract

While deep learning has revolutionized protein structure prediction, almost all experimentally characterized de novo protein designs have been generated using physically based approaches such as Rosetta. Here we describe a deep learning based protein sequence design method, ProteinMPNN, with outstanding performance in both in silico and experimental tests. # ProteinMPNN: Robust Deep Learning–Based Protein Sequence Design

## Structured Scientific Review

---

**Source Paper**
- Title: Robust deep learning–based protein sequence design using ProteinMPNN
- Authors: Dauparas J, Anishchenko I, Bennett N, Bai H, Ragotte RJ, Milles LF, Wicky BIM, Courbet A, de Haas RJ, Bethel N, Leung PJY, Huddy TF, Pellock S, Tischer D, Chan F, Koepnick B, Nguyen H, Kang A, Sankaran B, Bera AK, King NP, Baker D
- Journal: *Science*, 378(6615), 49–56 (2022)
- DOI: [10.1126/science.add2187](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add2187)
- PMID: [36108050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36108050/)
- Preprint: [10.1101/2022.06.03.494563](https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.06.03.494563) (bioRxiv, CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0)
- Code: [github.com/dauparas/ProteinMPNN](https://github.com/dauparas/ProteinMPNN)
- PDB ID of solved crystal structure: 8CYK

**Review Coverage Note**: This structured review is based on the openly accessible bioRxiv preprint (version 1, posted 2022-06-04). The published *Science* version (2022-10-07) is behind a paywall and was not accessible for full-text verification. Numerical values and methodological details cited below are drawn from the preprint and its Supplementary Materials. Any discrepancies between the preprint and the final published version cannot be assessed here.

---

## Abstract

Protein sequence design—determining an amino acid sequence that folds into a given target backbone—has historically relied on physics-based energy optimization engines such as Rosetta. Recent deep learning approaches have shown promise for monomer design but have remained limited in scope and lacked rigorous experimental validation. Dauparas et al. present ProteinMPNN, a message-passing neural network designed to operate across monomers, cyclic oligomers, protein nanoparticles, and protein–protein interfaces. On native protein backbones, ProteinMPNN attains an overall sequence recovery of 52.4% versus 32.9% for Rosetta, while requiring only 1.2 seconds per 100-residue protein on a single CPU compared to approximately 259 seconds for Rosetta. Training with backbone coordinate noise improves structural robustness assessed by single-sequence AlphaFold predictions: a model trained with 0.3 Å noise yields 2–3 times more sequences within an lDDT-Cα threshold of 95.0 compared to un-noised models. Experimentally, ProteinMPNN rescues previously failed designs generated with Rosetta or AlphaFold. In one representative experiment, of 96 ProteinMPNN designs expressed in *E. coli*, 73 were soluble (median yield = 247 mg/L versus 9 mg/L for the original AlphaFold sequences), and 50 exhibited the target oligomeric state by size-exclusion chromatography. X-ray crystallography (monomer, RMSD = 2.35 Å over 130 residues; tetrahedral nanoparticle, 1.2 Å Cα RMSD) and cryo-EM structures confirm high structural fidelity. The method requires no manual intervention for specific design tasks, making protein sequence design more broadly accessible.

---

## Introduction

The central challenge in computational protein design is the inverse folding problem: given a three-dimensional protein backbone, identify an amino acid sequence that will spontaneously adopt that structure. For two decades, Rosetta and related physically based tools have dominated this field, treating sequence design as a combinatorial energy-minimization problem in which side-chain conformations (rotamers) are packed onto a fixed backbone and scored with an all-atom energy function. Despite notable successes, Rosetta-based design often requires expert customization—for instance, restricting hydrophobic residues on the solvent-exposed surface to suppress off-target oligomerization—and carries high computational cost due to the large search space of rotameric states.

In parallel, deep learning methods for protein sequence design have emerged (Ingraham et al. 2019; Anand et al. 2022), demonstrating the ability to rapidly propose plausible sequences from backbone geometry. However, these earlier methods focused primarily on the monomer design problem, achieved moderate native sequence recovery, and—with the exception of a TIM-barrel study (Anand et al. 2022)—remained largely unvalidated through high-resolution experimental structure determination. Moreover, challenges such as cyclic homo-oligomer design, repeat-protein design, symmetric nanoparticle assembly, and protein–protein interface design each demanded ad hoc adaptations of existing tools.

Dauparas and colleagues developed ProteinMPNN to address these gaps with a single, general-purpose framework. The key design objectives were: (i) high native sequence recovery on experimentally determined structures, (ii) robustness to backbone coordinate uncertainty, (iii) the ability to couple residue identities within and between chains for symmetry-aware design, (iv) order-agnostic decoding that accommodates fixed-context design scenarios, and (v) comprehensive experimental validation across diverse structural and functional challenges.

---

## Methods

### Model Architecture

ProteinMPNN is an encoder–decoder message-passing neural network (MPNN) with three encoder layers, three decoder layers, and a hidden dimension of 128. The encoder ingests backbone coordinates and outputs node and edge features; the decoder generates amino acid probabilities in an autoregressive fashion, conditioned on both the encoded structural features and the partially decoded sequence.

**Input features.** Edge features comprise 16 Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) equally spaced from 2 Å to 22 Å, encoding distances between N, Cα, C, O, and a virtual Cβ atom (computed from ideal backbone geometry) for residue pairs *i* and *j*. This yields 25 × 16 = 400 edge features. The virtual Cβ coordinates are defined as `Cβ = −0.58273431 × a + 0.56802827 × b − 0.54067466 × c + Cα`, where b = Cα − N, c = C − Cα, and a = cross(b, c). Relative positional encoding uses discrete one-hot tokens from −32 to +32 within a chain, plus a token for inter-chain residue pairs. No node input features are used, because including backbone dihedral angles as node features did not improve performance in preliminary tests on multi-chain backbones.

**Encoder with edge updates.** The encoder applies message passing with edge updates. For each residue pair, a message M<sub>ij</sub> is constructed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) applied to the concatenation of node features V<sub>i</sub>, V<sub>j</sub>, and edge features E<sub>ij</sub>. Messages are summed over neighbors and passed through another MLP to produce updated node representations, which in turn update edge representations. Layer normalization, dropout, and residual connections are used throughout.

**Order-agnostic decoding.** Instead of decoding from the N- to C-terminus, ProteinMPNN randomly permutes the decoding order during training (sampled uniformly from all possible permutations). This enables, at inference time, decoding that skips fixed-sequence regions while incorporating them as context—critical for protein binder design where the target-binding motif must be preserved.

**Positional coupling.** ProteinMPNN supports the tying of residue identities across equivalent positions within and between chains by averaging predicted logits over the tied set before sampling from the joint probability distribution. This enables symmetry-constrained design (e.g., C<sub>n</sub> homo-oligomers), repeat-protein design, and multi-state design where logits from different backbone conformations are averaged to produce a single consensus sequence.

**Noise-augmented training.** During training, Gaussian noise can be added to backbone atomic coordinates. The standard deviation of the noise is a tunable hyperparameter; models were trained with noise levels from 0.02 Å to 0.3 Å. All evaluations in the paper use unperturbed backbone coordinates at test time unless specified otherwise.

### Training Data and Procedure

**Single-chain models.** The dataset was constructed from the CATH 4.2 40% non-redundant set of protein domains, comprising 19,700 high-resolution single-chain structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), split according to CATH topology classification. Training hyperparameters: dropout rate 10%, label smoothing 10%, batch size 6,000 tokens, graph sparsity set to 30 nearest neighbors by Cα–Cα distance, and the learning-rate schedule from Vaswani et al. (2017).

**Multi-chain ProteinMPNN.** Training data were all PDB biological assemblies (as of 2021-08-02) determined by X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM to better than 3.5 Å resolution with fewer than 10,000 residues. Sequences were clustered at 30% sequence identity with MMseqs2, yielding 25,361 clusters. Clusters were randomly split into training (23,358), validation (1,464), and test (1,539) sets, ensuring that no chain or its biological assembly partners appeared in more than one split. At each training epoch, one random member was drawn per cluster; for entries with multiple conformations or assemblies, one was selected at random. For hetero-oligomers, the query chain's sequence was masked while partner-chain sequences were provided to the network; for homo-oligomers (pairwise sequence identity > 70% by TM-align), sequences of all copies were masked to prevent information leakage.

**Loss function and optimization.** The loss is the sum of per-token categorical cross-entropy divided by 2,000 (an empirically chosen normalizer), with label smoothing at 10%. The optimizer is Adam (β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98, ε = 10⁻⁹) with the Transformer learning-rate schedule. Training used a batch size of 10,000 tokens, automatic mixed precision, and gradient checkpointing on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Validation perplexity converged at approximately 150,000 optimizer steps (~100 epochs).

### In Silico Benchmarks

Native sequence recovery was evaluated on test sets of 690 monomers, 732 homo-oligomers (<2,000 residues), and 98 hetero-oligomers. Rosetta comparison used one round of the PackRotamersMover with the beta_nov16 score function on a set of 402 monomer backbones.

Structural encoding fidelity was assessed by completely redesigning 396 monomer structures (max 300 residues) and 277 homo-oligomer structures (max 400 residues) with ProteinMPNN, then running single-sequence AlphaFold (5 models, 3 recycles, selecting the highest-average-pLDDT model) on the resulting sequences. For de novo scaffold redesign, approximately 3,000 previously Rosetta-designed NTF2-fold backbones were re-sequenced with ProteinMPNN and evaluated analogously.

Sequence recovery on AlphaFold-generated structure models was measured using 5,000 UniRef50 sequences with average pLDDT > 80.0, and the correlation between sequence recovery and confidence was evaluated on 1,621 such models (Spearman ρ = 0.502 between recovery and pLDDT).

### Experimental Validation

**Expression and solubility.** Synthetic genes encoding designed sequences were expressed in *E. coli*. Soluble yield was quantified from the integrated area under size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) traces of Ni-NTA purified proteins.

**Structural characterization.** X-ray crystallography was performed on select designs; one monomer (LM0878; PDB 8CYK) was crystallized in 0.1 M citric acid pH 3.5 and 3 M NaCl, with diffraction data collected at 100 K at ALS beamline 8.2.1. Data were integrated with XDS, scaled with Aimless, and phased by molecular replacement with Phaser; refinement was done with Coot and Phenix. Ten cyclic homo-oligomer structures were determined by cryo-EM (accompanying manuscript, Wicky et al.). Negative-stain electron microscopy was used for C5/C6 cyclic oligomers.

**Biophysical characterization.** Thermostability was assessed by circular dichroism spectroscopy from 25 °C to 95 °C. Oligomeric state was confirmed by SEC and SEC-MALS. For the functional design test, binding of Grb2 SH3-domain scaffolding proteins was measured by biolayer interferometry.

### Design Tasks Evaluated

1. **Monomer and homo-oligomer design** (AlphaFold-hallucinated backbones): 96 backbones redesigned.
2. **Repeat-protein design** (Rosetta DHR82 scaffold): residues tied at corresponding repeat positions.
3. **Cyclic oligomer design with internal repeats** (C5/C6 symmetries): positions tied both within and between subunits.
4. **Two-component tetrahedral nanoparticle design**: 76 sequences spanning 27 previously described tetrahedral backbones (King et al. 2014); identities tied at equivalent positions across 12 subunit copies per assembly.
5. **Protein function design** (Grb2 SH3-domain binding): helical scaffolds docking a polyproline-rich peptide recognized by Grb2; point mutations (asparagine → aspartate) introduced as specificity controls.

---

## Results

### In Silico Performance

On the 402-monomer test set, ProteinMPNN achieved 52.4% overall native sequence recovery versus 32.9% for Rosetta, with improvements observed at all levels of residue burial (core through surface). The time per 100-residue design was 1.2 seconds (ProteinMPNN; single CPU) compared to 258.8 seconds (Rosetta).

For the multi-chain test sets, median sequence recoveries were 52% (690 monomers), 55% (732 homo-oligomers), and 51% (98 hetero-oligomers). Recovery correlated with burial depth, ranging from approximately 90–95% in the deep core to approximately 35% on the surface. For homo-oligomers, averaging logits between symmetry-related positions yielded the highest recovery (55%) versus unconstrained design (52%) or probability averaging (53%).

**Noise training and AlphaFold decoding.** Native sequence recovery on perfect backbones decreased with increasing training noise, as these models lost sensitivity to fine backbone details. However, sequences from noised models were far more accurately decoded into three-dimensional coordinates by single-sequence AlphaFold. A model trained with 0.3 Å noise produced 2–3 times more sequences within lDDT-Cα thresholds of 90.0 and 95.0 compared to un-noised or lightly noised (0.02 Å) models. Training with 0.02 Å noise improved sequence recovery on AlphaFold-predicted backbone models (average pLDDT > 80.0) relative to models trained only on perfect coordinates. For monomer sequences redesigned from 396 native structures, single-sequence AlphaFold predictions of ProteinMPNN-designed sequences matched the original native backbones more confidently and accurately than predictions from the original native sequences.

**De novo scaffold rescue.** ProteinMPNN redesign of approximately 3,000 previously Rosetta-designed NTF2-fold backbones substantially increased the fraction of sequences predicted by single-sequence AlphaFold to fold to the target structures.

**Sequence diversity.** Inference temperature modulated the diversity–accuracy trade-off; higher temperatures (above the default T = 0.1) substantially increased sequence diversity with only a modest decrease in average recovery. The average log-probability of the sequence given the structure correlated strongly with native sequence recovery across temperatures, providing a ranking criterion for experimental candidate selection.

### Experimental Validation

**Monomer and oligomer rescue.** AlphaFold-hallucinated sequences were mostly insoluble when expressed in *E. coli* (median soluble yield: 9 mg/L culture equivalent; N = 150 attempted expressions). ProteinMPNN redesign of a subset of these backbones raised the success rate dramatically: 73 of 96 designs (76%) were soluble (median yield: 247 mg/L), and 50 showed the target monomeric or oligomeric state by SEC. Many designs retained secondary structure up to 95 °C as assessed by circular dichroism. One monomer structure (PDB 8CYK) was solved by X-ray crystallography at 2.35 Å RMSD over 130 residues relative to the design model; AlphaFold-predicted side chains from the ProteinMPNN sequence fit nearly perfectly into the experimental electron density in the hydrophobic core.

**Repeat proteins.** Previous Rosetta repeat-protein designs (e.g., DHR82) were rescued by ProteinMPNN redesign with tied residue identities. SEC profiles showed sharp monodisperse peaks at the expected retention volume for the ProteinMPNN variants, in contrast to the poorly behaved Rosetta designs.

**Cyclic oligomers with internal repeats.** In a set of C5/C6 cyclic oligomers: Rosetta-designed sequences showed 40% soluble expression and none confirmed in the correct oligomeric state by SEC-MALS; ProteinMPNN-designed sequences showed 88% soluble expression and 27.7% correct oligomeric state. Negative-stain EM class averages of one such design matched the design model closely.

**Tetrahedral nanoparticles.** Of 76 ProteinMPNN designs spanning 27 two-component tetrahedral backbones, 13 formed assemblies with the expected molecular weight (~1 MDa) by SEC. A crystal structure of one previously failed Rosetta design (T33-27) yielded a 1.2 Å Cα RMSD over two subunits compared to the design model.

**Functional protein design.** ProteinMPNN sequences designed for backbones scaffolding a Grb2 SH3-domain-binding proline-rich peptide showed strong binding by biolayer interferometry—considerably higher signal than the free peptide alone. The original Rosetta-designed sequences for the same backbones showed no binding. Introduction of two point mutations (asparagine → aspartate) predicted to disrupt the scaffold–peptide interface eliminated the binding signal.

---

## Discussion

ProteinMPNN departs from the Rosetta paradigm by directly learning the conditional distribution of amino acids given backbone geometry, rather than solving a proxy energy minimization. This has several consequences observed in the study.

First, ProteinMPNN eliminates the need for expert heuristic tuning. In Rosetta, hydrophobic residues must often be manually penalized on exposed surfaces, and the transition zone between core and surface introduces ambiguity about the extent of such constraints. ProteinMPNN implicitly learns context-appropriate amino acid preferences from the PDB without requiring such rules.

Second, noise-augmented training decouples two often-conflated objectives: maximizing native sequence recovery on crystallographic coordinates versus generating sequences that robustly encode the target fold under structural uncertainty. The authors argue that crystal structures may carry subtle "memory" of the amino acid identity in their refined coordinates—a bias exploited by models trained on perfect backbones but absent from predicted structures. Noise-trained models, by attending to global topology rather than local coordinate fine structure, generate sequences that are more faithfully decoded by structure prediction algorithms and, as the experimental data suggest, more likely to fold correctly in practice.

Third, the study contributes a quantitative demonstration that single-sequence AlphaFold predictions can serve as a screening tool for designed sequences—a workflow that was not feasible with earlier design methods whose sequences rarely passed such filters.

**Numerical relationship between in silico metrics and experimental success.** One notable finding is that the strength of the single-sequence–to–structure mapping, quantified by the fraction of sequences reaching high AlphaFold confidence thresholds, is a more predictive operational metric for experimental success than native sequence recovery alone. Models trained with 0.3 Å noise achieved the best lDDT-Cα decoding success despite lower native sequence recovery, and the resulting sequences performed well experimentally.

### Limitations

The following constraints are either stated explicitly in the preprint or logically follow from the reported methods and results.

1. **No dedicated "Limitations" section exists.** The caveats below are drawn from statements distributed across the Conclusion and Supplementary Methods.

2. **Physical interpretability.** The authors acknowledge that deep learning methods, including ProteinMPNN, lack the physical transparency of Rosetta. The reasoning behind a specific sequence choice is not provided by an interpretable energy decomposition.

3. **In silico metrics are resolution-dependent.** Native sequence recovery correlates inversely with PDB crystallographic resolution (Spearman ρ = −0.487 across 690 monomers), so the benchmark is sensitive to training-data quality.

4. **Sequence recovery does not guarantee folding.** Even a single amino acid substitution can abrogate folding while leaving overall sequence recovery nearly unchanged. Experimental validation remains the definitive test, analogous to how automated translation quality must ultimately be evaluated by human readers.

5. **Structural validation depends on AlphaFold's single-sequence capability.** The paper shows that AlphaFold single-sequence success rates improve with the number of recycles (tested up to 12), but remain limited. Stronger single-sequence structure predictors would likely reveal even higher success rates for ProteinMPNN designs.

6. **Domain scope.** At the time of reporting, the method was being extended to protein–nucleic acid and protein–small molecule design; these modalities were not yet validated.

7. **Experimental sample sizes are modest for some endpoints.** For example, the crystal structure confirmation of the tetrahedral nanoparticle covers one design (T33-27), the monomer crystal structure covers one design (LM0878, PDB 8CYK), and the Grb2 functional validation covers one design scaffold. The cryo-EM dataset of ten cyclic homo-oligomers is reported in an accompanying manuscript and was not independently assessed here.

8. **Preprint status.** This review is based on the bioRxiv preprint (version 1). The published *Science* article may contain additional experiments, revised figures, or updated numerical values that could not be verified.

9. **No negative control for solubility rescue.** While the comparison between original AlphaFold-hallucinated sequences (N = 150 attempted, median yield 9 mg/L) and ProteinMPNN variants (N = 96, median yield 247 mg/L) is striking, the two sets were not randomly drawn from the same hallucinated backbone population; a subset of backbones was selected for ProteinMPNN rescue.

---

## Conclusion

ProteinMPNN is a general-purpose deep learning method for protein sequence design that outperforms Rosetta in native sequence recovery (52.4% vs. 32.9%), computational speed (~200-fold faster), and—most critically—experimental success rate across a panel of previously failed protein designs spanning monomers, cyclic homo-oligomers, repeat proteins, tetrahedral nanoparticles, and protein–protein interfaces. It requires no manual customization per design task. The method has been adopted as the standard sequence-design workflow at the Institute for Protein Design and has been released as open-source software. Its demonstrated ability to rescue failed Rosetta and AlphaFold designs, combined with the observation that ProteinMPNN-designed sequences are more confidently and accurately decoded by single-sequence AlphaFold than native sequences, suggests broad utility for both de novo design and the stabilization of recombinantly expressed natural proteins.

## Abstract

Protein sequence design—determining an amino acid sequence that folds into a given target backbone—has historically relied on physics-based energy optimization engines such as Rosetta. Recent deep learning approaches have shown promise for monomer design but have remained limited in scope and lacked rigorous experimental validation. Dauparas et al. present ProteinMPNN, a message-passing neural network designed to operate across monomers, cyclic oligomers, protein nanoparticles, and protein–protein interfaces. On native protein backbones, ProteinMPNN attains an overall sequence recovery of 52.4% versus 32.9% for Rosetta, while requiring only 1.2 seconds per 100-residue protein on a single CPU compared to approximately 259 seconds for Rosetta. Training with backbone coordinate noise improves structural robustness assessed by single-sequence AlphaFold predictions: a model trained with 0.3 Å noise yields 2–3 times more sequences within an lDDT-Cα threshold of 95.0 compared to un-noised models. Experimentally, ProteinMPNN rescues previously failed designs generated with Rosetta or AlphaFold. In one representative experiment, of 96 ProteinMPNN designs expressed in *E. coli*, 73 were soluble (median yield = 247 mg/L versus 9 mg/L for the original AlphaFold sequences), and 50 exhibited the target oligomeric state by size-exclusion chromatography. X-ray crystallography (monomer, RMSD = 2.35 Å over 130 residues; tetrahedral nanoparticle, 1.2 Å Cα RMSD) and cryo-EM structures confirm high structural fidelity. The method requires no manual intervention for specific design tasks, making protein sequence design more broadly accessible.

## Introduction

The central challenge in computational protein design is the inverse folding problem: given a three-dimensional protein backbone, identify an amino acid sequence that will spontaneously adopt that structure. For two decades, Rosetta and related physically based tools have dominated this field, treating sequence design as a combinatorial energy-minimization problem in which side-chain conformations (rotamers) are packed onto a fixed backbone and scored with an all-atom energy function. Despite notable successes, Rosetta-based design often requires expert customization—for instance, restricting hydrophobic residues on the solvent-exposed surface to suppress off-target oligomerization—and carries high computational cost due to the large search space of rotameric states.

In parallel, deep learning methods for protein sequence design have emerged (Ingraham et al. 2019; Anand et al. 2022), demonstrating the ability to rapidly propose plausible sequences from backbone geometry. However, these earlier methods focused primarily on the monomer design problem, achieved moderate native sequence recovery, and—with the exception of a TIM-barrel study (Anand et al. 2022)—remained largely unvalidated through high-resolution experimental structure determination. Moreover, challenges such as cyclic homo-oligomer design, repeat-protein design, symmetric nanoparticle assembly, and protein–protein interface design each demanded ad hoc adaptations of existing tools.

Dauparas and colleagues developed ProteinMPNN to address these gaps with a single, general-purpose framework. The key design objectives were: (i) high native sequence recovery on experimentally determined structures, (ii) robustness to backbone coordinate uncertainty, (iii) the ability to couple residue identities within and between chains for symmetry-aware design, (iv) order-agnostic decoding that accommodates fixed-context design scenarios, and (v) comprehensive experimental validation across diverse structural and functional challenges.

## Methods

### Model Architecture

ProteinMPNN is an encoder–decoder message-passing neural network (MPNN) with three encoder layers, three decoder layers, and a hidden dimension of 128. The encoder ingests backbone coordinates and outputs node and edge features; the decoder generates amino acid probabilities in an autoregressive fashion, conditioned on both the encoded structural features and the partially decoded sequence.

**Input features.** Edge features comprise 16 Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) equally spaced from 2 Å to 22 Å, encoding distances between N, Cα, C, O, and a virtual Cβ atom (computed from ideal backbone geometry) for residue pairs *i* and *j*. This yields 25 × 16 = 400 edge features. The virtual Cβ coordinates are defined as `Cβ = −0.58273431 × a + 0.56802827 × b − 0.54067466 × c + Cα`, where b = Cα − N, c = C − Cα, and a = cross(b, c). Relative positional encoding uses discrete one-hot tokens from −32 to +32 within a chain, plus a token for inter-chain residue pairs. No node input features are used, because including backbone dihedral angles as node features did not improve performance in preliminary tests on multi-chain backbones.

**Encoder with edge updates.** The encoder applies message passing with edge updates. For each residue pair, a message M<sub>ij</sub> is constructed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) applied to the concatenation of node features V<sub>i</sub>, V<sub>j</sub>, and edge features E<sub>ij</sub>. Messages are summed over neighbors and passed through another MLP to produce updated node representations, which in turn update edge representations. Layer normalization, dropout, and residual connections are used throughout.

**Order-agnostic decoding.** Instead of decoding from the N- to C-terminus, ProteinMPNN randomly permutes the decoding order during training (sampled uniformly from all possible permutations). This enables, at inference time, decoding that skips fixed-sequence regions while incorporating them as context—critical for protein binder design where the target-binding motif must be preserved.

**Positional coupling.** ProteinMPNN supports the tying of residue identities across equivalent positions within and between chains by averaging predicted logits over the tied set before sampling from the joint probability distribution. This enables symmetry-constrained design (e.g., C<sub>n</sub> homo-oligomers), repeat-protein design, and multi-state design where logits from different backbone conformations are averaged to produce a single consensus sequence.

**Noise-augmented training.** During training, Gaussian noise can be added to backbone atomic coordinates. The standard deviation of the noise is a tunable hyperparameter; models were trained with noise levels from 0.02 Å to 0.3 Å. All evaluations in the paper use unperturbed backbone coordinates at test time unless specified otherwise.

### Training Data and Procedure

**Single-chain models.** The dataset was constructed from the CATH 4.2 40% non-redundant set of protein domains, comprising 19,700 high-resolution single-chain structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), split according to CATH topology classification. Training hyperparameters: dropout rate 10%, label smoothing 10%, batch size 6,000 tokens, graph sparsity set to 30 nearest neighbors by Cα–Cα distance, and the learning-rate schedule from Vaswani et al. (2017).

**Multi-chain ProteinMPNN.** Training data were all PDB biological assemblies (as of 2021-08-02) determined by X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM to better than 3.5 Å resolution with fewer than 10,000 residues. Sequences were clustered at 30% sequence identity with MMseqs2, yielding 25,361 clusters. Clusters were randomly split into training (23,358), validation (1,464), and test (1,539) sets, ensuring that no chain or its biological assembly partners appeared in more than one split. At each training epoch, one random member was drawn per cluster; for entries with multiple conformations or assemblies, one was selected at random. For hetero-oligomers, the query chain's sequence was masked while partner-chain sequences were provided to the network; for homo-oligomers (pairwise sequence identity > 70% by TM-align), sequences of all copies were masked to prevent information leakage.

**Loss function and optimization.** The loss is the sum of per-token categorical cross-entropy divided by 2,000 (an empirically chosen normalizer), with label smoothing at 10%. The optimizer is Adam (β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98, ε = 10⁻⁹) with the Transformer learning-rate schedule. Training used a batch size of 10,000 tokens, automatic mixed precision, and gradient checkpointing on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Validation perplexity converged at approximately 150,000 optimizer steps (~100 epochs).

### In Silico Benchmarks

Native sequence recovery was evaluated on test sets of 690 monomers, 732 homo-oligomers (<2,000 residues), and 98 hetero-oligomers. Rosetta comparison used one round of the PackRotamersMover with the beta_nov16 score function on a set of 402 monomer backbones.

Structural encoding fidelity was assessed by completely redesigning 396 monomer structures (max 300 residues) and 277 homo-oligomer structures (max 400 residues) with ProteinMPNN, then running single-sequence AlphaFold (5 models, 3 recycles, selecting the highest-average-pLDDT model) on the resulting sequences. For de novo scaffold redesign, approximately 3,000 previously Rosetta-designed NTF2-fold backbones were re-sequenced with ProteinMPNN and evaluated analogously.

Sequence recovery on AlphaFold-generated structure models was measured using 5,000 UniRef50 sequences with average pLDDT > 80.0, and the correlation between sequence recovery and confidence was evaluated on 1,621 such models (Spearman ρ = 0.502 between recovery and pLDDT).

### Experimental Validation

**Expression and solubility.** Synthetic genes encoding designed sequences were expressed in *E. coli*. Soluble yield was quantified from the integrated area under size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) traces of Ni-NTA purified proteins.

**Structural characterization.** X-ray crystallography was performed on select designs; one monomer (LM0878; PDB 8CYK) was crystallized in 0.1 M citric acid pH 3.5 and 3 M NaCl, with diffraction data collected at 100 K at ALS beamline 8.2.1. Data were integrated with XDS, scaled with Aimless, and phased by molecular replacement with Phaser; refinement was done with Coot and Phenix. Ten cyclic homo-oligomer structures were determined by cryo-EM (accompanying manuscript, Wicky et al.). Negative-stain electron microscopy was used for C5/C6 cyclic oligomers.

**Biophysical characterization.** Thermostability was assessed by circular dichroism spectroscopy from 25 °C to 95 °C. Oligomeric state was confirmed by SEC and SEC-MALS. For the functional design test, binding of Grb2 SH3-domain scaffolding proteins was measured by biolayer interferometry.

### Design Tasks Evaluated

1. **Monomer and homo-oligomer design** (AlphaFold-hallucinated backbones): 96 backbones redesigned.
2. **Repeat-protein design** (Rosetta DHR82 scaffold): residues tied at corresponding repeat positions.
3. **Cyclic oligomer design with internal repeats** (C5/C6 symmetries): positions tied both within and between subunits.
4. **Two-component tetrahedral nanoparticle design**: 76 sequences spanning 27 previously described tetrahedral backbones (King et al. 2014); identities tied at equivalent positions across 12 subunit copies per assembly.
5. **Protein function design** (Grb2 SH3-domain binding): helical scaffolds docking a polyproline-rich peptide recognized by Grb2; point mutations (asparagine → aspartate) introduced as specificity controls.

## Results

### In Silico Performance

On the 402-monomer test set, ProteinMPNN achieved 52.4% overall native sequence recovery versus 32.9% for Rosetta, with improvements observed at all levels of residue burial (core through surface). The time per 100-residue design was 1.2 seconds (ProteinMPNN; single CPU) compared to 258.8 seconds (Rosetta).

For the multi-chain test sets, median sequence recoveries were 52% (690 monomers), 55% (732 homo-oligomers), and 51% (98 hetero-oligomers). Recovery correlated with burial depth, ranging from approximately 90–95% in the deep core to approximately 35% on the surface. For homo-oligomers, averaging logits between symmetry-related positions yielded the highest recovery (55%) versus unconstrained design (52%) or probability averaging (53%).

**Noise training and AlphaFold decoding.** Native sequence recovery on perfect backbones decreased with increasing training noise, as these models lost sensitivity to fine backbone details. However, sequences from noised models were far more accurately decoded into three-dimensional coordinates by single-sequence AlphaFold. A model trained with 0.3 Å noise produced 2–3 times more sequences within lDDT-Cα thresholds of 90.0 and 95.0 compared to un-noised or lightly noised (0.02 Å) models. Training with 0.02 Å noise improved sequence recovery on AlphaFold-predicted backbone models (average pLDDT > 80.0) relative to models trained only on perfect coordinates. For monomer sequences redesigned from 396 native structures, single-sequence AlphaFold predictions of ProteinMPNN-designed sequences matched the original native backbones more confidently and accurately than predictions from the original native sequences.

**De novo scaffold rescue.** ProteinMPNN redesign of approximately 3,000 previously Rosetta-designed NTF2-fold backbones substantially increased the fraction of sequences predicted by single-sequence AlphaFold to fold to the target structures.

**Sequence diversity.** Inference temperature modulated the diversity–accuracy trade-off; higher temperatures (above the default T = 0.1) substantially increased sequence diversity with only a modest decrease in average recovery. The average log-probability of the sequence given the structure correlated strongly with native sequence recovery across temperatures, providing a ranking criterion for experimental candidate selection.

### Experimental Validation

**Monomer and oligomer rescue.** AlphaFold-hallucinated sequences were mostly insoluble when expressed in *E. coli* (median soluble yield: 9 mg/L culture equivalent; N = 150 attempted expressions). ProteinMPNN redesign of a subset of these backbones raised the success rate dramatically: 73 of 96 designs (76%) were soluble (median yield: 247 mg/L), and 50 showed the target monomeric or oligomeric state by SEC. Many designs retained secondary structure up to 95 °C as assessed by circular dichroism. One monomer structure (PDB 8CYK) was solved by X-ray crystallography at 2.35 Å RMSD over 130 residues relative to the design model; AlphaFold-predicted side chains from the ProteinMPNN sequence fit nearly perfectly into the experimental electron density in the hydrophobic core.

**Repeat proteins.** Previous Rosetta repeat-protein designs (e.g., DHR82) were rescued by ProteinMPNN redesign with tied residue identities. SEC profiles showed sharp monodisperse peaks at the expected retention volume for the ProteinMPNN variants, in contrast to the poorly behaved Rosetta designs.

**Cyclic oligomers with internal repeats.** In a set of C5/C6 cyclic oligomers: Rosetta-designed sequences showed 40% soluble expression and none confirmed in the correct oligomeric state by SEC-MALS; ProteinMPNN-designed sequences showed 88% soluble expression and 27.7% correct oligomeric state. Negative-stain EM class averages of one such design matched the design model closely.

**Tetrahedral nanoparticles.** Of 76 ProteinMPNN designs spanning 27 two-component tetrahedral backbones, 13 formed assemblies with the expected molecular weight (~1 MDa) by SEC. A crystal structure of one previously failed Rosetta design (T33-27) yielded a 1.2 Å Cα RMSD over two subunits compared to the design model.

**Functional protein design.** ProteinMPNN sequences designed for backbones scaffolding a Grb2 SH3-domain-binding proline-rich peptide showed strong binding by biolayer interferometry—considerably higher signal than the free peptide alone. The original Rosetta-designed sequences for the same backbones showed no binding. Introduction of two point mutations (asparagine → aspartate) predicted to disrupt the scaffold–peptide interface eliminated the binding signal.

## Discussion

ProteinMPNN departs from the Rosetta paradigm by directly learning the conditional distribution of amino acids given backbone geometry, rather than solving a proxy energy minimization. This has several consequences observed in the study.

First, ProteinMPNN eliminates the need for expert heuristic tuning. In Rosetta, hydrophobic residues must often be manually penalized on exposed surfaces, and the transition zone between core and surface introduces ambiguity about the extent of such constraints. ProteinMPNN implicitly learns context-appropriate amino acid preferences from the PDB without requiring such rules.

Second, noise-augmented training decouples two often-conflated objectives: maximizing native sequence recovery on crystallographic coordinates versus generating sequences that robustly encode the target fold under structural uncertainty. The authors argue that crystal structures may carry subtle "memory" of the amino acid identity in their refined coordinates—a bias exploited by models trained on perfect backbones but absent from predicted structures. Noise-trained models, by attending to global topology rather than local coordinate fine structure, generate sequences that are more faithfully decoded by structure prediction algorithms and, as the experimental data suggest, more likely to fold correctly in practice.

Third, the study contributes a quantitative demonstration that single-sequence AlphaFold predictions can serve as a screening tool for designed sequences—a workflow that was not feasible with earlier design methods whose sequences rarely passed such filters.

**Numerical relationship between in silico metrics and experimental success.** One notable finding is that the strength of the single-sequence–to–structure mapping, quantified by the fraction of sequences reaching high AlphaFold confidence thresholds, is a more predictive operational metric for experimental success than native sequence recovery alone. Models trained with 0.3 Å noise achieved the best lDDT-Cα decoding success despite lower native sequence recovery, and the resulting sequences performed well experimentally.

### Limitations

The following constraints are either stated explicitly in the preprint or logically follow from the reported methods and results.

1. **No dedicated "Limitations" section exists.** The caveats below are drawn from statements distributed across the Conclusion and Supplementary Methods.

2. **Physical interpretability.** The authors acknowledge that deep learning methods, including ProteinMPNN, lack the physical transparency of Rosetta. The reasoning behind a specific sequence choice is not provided by an interpretable energy decomposition.

3. **In silico metrics are resolution-dependent.** Native sequence recovery correlates inversely with PDB crystallographic resolution (Spearman ρ = −0.487 across 690 monomers), so the benchmark is sensitive to training-data quality.

4. **Sequence recovery does not guarantee folding.** Even a single amino acid substitution can abrogate folding while leaving overall sequence recovery nearly unchanged. Experimental validation remains the definitive test, analogous to how automated translation quality must ultimately be evaluated by human readers.

5. **Structural validation depends on AlphaFold's single-sequence capability.** The paper shows that AlphaFold single-sequence success rates improve with the number of recycles (tested up to 12), but remain limited. Stronger single-sequence structure predictors would likely reveal even higher success rates for ProteinMPNN designs.

6. **Domain scope.** At the time of reporting, the method was being extended to protein–nucleic acid and protein–small molecule design; these modalities were not yet validated.

7. **Experimental sample sizes are modest for some endpoints.** For example, the crystal structure confirmation of the tetrahedral nanoparticle covers one design (T33-27), the monomer crystal structure covers one design (LM0878, PDB 8CYK), and the Grb2 functional validation covers one design scaffold. The cryo-EM dataset of ten cyclic homo-oligomers is reported in an accompanying manuscript and was not independently assessed here.

8. **Preprint status.** This review is based on the bioRxiv preprint (version 1). The published *Science* article may contain additional experiments, revised figures, or updated numerical values that could not be verified.

9. **No negative control for solubility rescue.** While the comparison between original AlphaFold-hallucinated sequences (N = 150 attempted, median yield 9 mg/L) and ProteinMPNN variants (N = 96, median yield 247 mg/L) is striking, the two sets were not randomly drawn from the same hallucinated backbone population; a subset of backbones was selected for ProteinMPNN rescue.

## Conclusion

ProteinMPNN is a general-purpose deep learning method for protein sequence design that outperforms Rosetta in native sequence recovery (52.4% vs. 32.9%), computational speed (~200-fold faster), and—most critically—experimental success rate across a panel of previously failed protein designs spanning monomers, cyclic homo-oligomers, repeat proteins, tetrahedral nanoparticles, and protein–protein interfaces. It requires no manual customization per design task. The method has been adopted as the standard sequence-design workflow at the Institute for Protein Design and has been released as open-source software. Its demonstrated ability to rescue failed Rosetta and AlphaFold designs, combined with the observation that ProteinMPNN-designed sequences are more confidently and accurately decoded by single-sequence AlphaFold than native sequences, suggests broad utility for both de novo design and the stabilization of recombinantly expressed natural proteins.
